Two-year-old Areesha Shehzad from Bradford is fighting for her life with Crigler-Najjar syndrome type 1 â a condition so rare that fewer than 200 people worldwide have it. Her body cannot break down bilirubin, a toxic byproduct of red blood cell breakdown, which builds up and threatens irreversible brain damage. To survive, she must spend at least 12 hours every day lying under special blue phototherapy lights that help neutralize the toxin through her skin.

These lights, which glow intensely in her custom-built cot, allow her to stay alive â but at a heavy cost. Nighttime sleep is nearly impossible, leaving Areesha exhausted during the day. She misses out on playdates, toddler groups, and the simple joys of childhood, often playing alone while the lights keep her awake. Her parents, Majid and Salma, describe the daily struggle as heartbreaking. 'It feels like a prison,' says Majid. 'We have to force her to stay there, and explaining that to a toddler breaks our hearts.'

Diagnosed after initial confusion with newborn jaundice, Areesha spent four months in hospital before doctors confirmed the rare syndrome. Since then, phototherapy has kept her bilirubin levels at a dangerous but manageable 300 â far above the normal range of 5 to 20. If levels climb past 450, seizures and permanent brain injury become likely. Her consultant, Dr. Patricia McClean, says sheâs seen only half a dozen cases like Areeshaâs in her 20-year career.

As Areesha grows, her skin thickens, reducing the therapyâs effectiveness. Soon, sheâll need 16 or more hours daily under the lights. The only long-term solution? A liver transplant. Preliminary tests are scheduled next month at Leeds General Infirmary, and her father is being evaluated as a possible donor. Despite the overwhelming challenges, her family holds onto hope â determined to give Areesha as normal a childhood as possible, even if it means living under blue lights most of the day.

In Des Moines, Iowa, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton is once again drawing attention as potential Democratic candidates gear up for the 2016 race. At the annual Harkin Steak Fry, she subtly signaled renewed interest in the presidency â a move that has reignited calls from her 2008 campaign team and local supporters to dominate the Iowa caucuses. Their argument? Win Iowa, and you lock up the nomination before the rest of the country even gets a chance to weigh in.

Jerry Crawford, who led Clintonâs Midwest efforts in 2008 and helped manage Bill Clintonâs Iowa campaigns in the â90s, says a strong win in the Hawkeye State would make it nearly impossible for any rival to catch up. Heâs shared this view directly with Clintonâs inner circle. For many of her backers, the stakes feel personal: in 2008, Clinton finished third in Iowa after a misstep involving a leaked memo suggesting she skip the state entirely. The incident damaged her image as a grounded candidate and allowed Barack Obama to surge ahead.

Now, polls show Clinton leading all potential Democratic contenders in Iowa with 53% support â triple the next closest candidate. Still, others are stepping onto the scene: Vice President Joe Biden spoke to nuns at the state capitol, Bernie Sanders held multiple rallies, and Maryland Governor Martin OâMalley has already deployed 11 staff members to the state.

Not everyone agrees that crushing the field in Iowa is the best path forward. Bonnie Campbell, Clintonâs 2008 co-chair and former head of the Iowa Democratic Party, believes healthy competition makes a candidate sharper. 'If she can beat them fairly and decisively here,' she says, 'then great. But we shouldnât fear debate â itâs part of democracy.'

Even Scott Brennan, chair of the Iowa Democratic Party, admits that an early Iowa victory could give Clinton a commanding national platform. Yet he also notes her 2008 loss wasnât due to lack of support â it was Obamaâs extraordinary campaign machine that overwhelmed her. Today, Clinton enters with far greater name recognition and resources. Whether she chooses to shut the door early or let the race breathe, Iowa will remain the ultimate proving ground.

Whether it was the way he chewed his cigar, shuffled for the paper in a bathrobe, or shifted from soothing tones to a guttural roar with his therapist, every detail felt real. David Chase, the creator of âThe Sopranos,â once told him, âYouâre like Mozart.â And maybe he was. Gandolfini passed away suddenly in Italy at age 51, likely from a heart attack, leaving behind a legacy that reshaped television.

Before âThe Sopranos,â Gandolfini was a respected but under-the-radar actorâonce a truck driver and bartenderâwho found his footing in theater and small film roles. He stood out even in minor parts, bringing depth to characters others might have overlooked. But it was Tony Soprano that changed everything: a mob boss who was also a confused, anxious father and husband. He wasnât just a criminalâhe was human, flawed, and achingly real.

The show itself defied categoriesâit couldâve been satire, soap opera, or crime thriller. But with Gandolfini at its center, it became something deeper: a slow-burning tragedy wrapped in dark humor. As Alan Sepinwall noted, Chase initially imagined the show as almost cartoonishâuntil he saw Gandolfiniâs performance and realized it had to be darker, grittier, more honest.

Gandolfini didnât rest on his fame. He turned down flashy Hollywood roles to appear in quieter films like âZero Dark Thirtyâ and âIn the Loop,â starred on Broadway in âGod of Carnage,â and even produced documentaries about veterans. In his final film, âNot Fade Away,â he played a weary New Jersey dad trying to understand his sonâs dreamsâand did it with heartbreaking tenderness, never overplaying it.

One of his most powerful moments? When Tony, comatose, imagines himself as a gentle optics salesman named Kevin Finnerty. No accent. No rage. Just vulnerability. Thatâs when you realized: Gandolfini wasnât Tony Soprano. He was an artist who could become anyoneâand made us believe every version.

Shaaliver Douse, 14, was killed by NYPD officers early Sunday in the Bronx. Police say he pointed a gun at them during a chase.

His mother, Shanise Farrar, spoke out Monday, defending her son: 'Iâm not saying heâs the best, but heâs my angel. I wouldnât want this to happen to anybodyâs kid.'

NYPD Commissioner Ray Kelly stated Shaaliver may be the youngest person ever killed by the NYPD. He defended the 26-year-old officer, who graduated from the police academy last month.

According to Kelly, Shaaliver fired multiple rounds and chased a man through the streets of the Bronx around 3 a.m. When officers confronted him, he refused to drop the pistol and pointed it at them. One officer fired a single shot, striking Shaaliver in the jaw and killing him.

Police sources told the New York Times that Shaaliver was likely pursuing a gang rival. Detectives believe the incident is connected to the May 24 shooting of a 15-year-old boy, only a mile and a half away â an incident in which Shaaliver was arrested and charged with attempted murder. Those charges were dropped after the victim could not identify him.

Shaaliver also faced a pending court date for a prior weapons possession arrest in October.

The NYPD released surveillance video showing a teen in a white T-shirt running toward a man outside a bodega and opening fire, followed by footage of him chasing the man around the corner. The same firearm â an Astra 9mm semiautomatic pistol â was recovered at the scene and shown with bloodstains.

Shaaliverâs family denies he was armed or involved in gangs. His aunt, Quwana Barcene, told the New York Post: 'Theyâre making it all up. There was no gun. Itâs all a cover-up. Itâs what the police do. They kill us and cover it up.'

Barcene compared the killing to that of Trayvon Martin and referenced the March 2013 death of 16-year-old Kimani Gray in Brooklyn, another case where police claimed the teen was armed.

The two officers involved â ages 26 and 27 â were part of an Operation Impact deployment in the high-crime neighborhood. The man Shaaliver was allegedly shooting at remains at large.

article_content: Human Rights Watch (HRW) reported on Thursday that Israel used white phosphorus in military operations across the Gaza Strip and along the Israel-Lebanon border. White phosphorus is an incendiary chemical that ignites upon contact with oxygen and can cause devastating burns when it touches human skin. It can also ignite buildings, crops, and other civilian infrastructure. HRW confirmed two videos showing white phosphorus being deployed over Gaza Cityâs port and rural areas near the Lebanese border. This comes amid Israelâs large-scale military response to Hamasâ deadly attacks on southern Israel on October 7, which killed approximately 1,300 people and resulted in the abduction of 100 to 150 hostages, including women, children, and elderly individuals. While white phosphorus is classified as an incendiary weapon â not a chemical weapon â its use in densely populated areas is prohibited under international humanitarian law. HRW concluded that Israelâs deployment of the substance in Gaza was unlawful. Lama Fakih, HRWâs Director for the Middle East and North Africa, stated, 'Any time white phosphorus is used in crowded civilian areas, it poses a high risk of excruciating burns and lifelong suffering.' She added that airburst use in urban zones is indiscriminate and can destroy homes and inflict catastrophic harm on civilians. This is not the first such accusation: HRW documented extensive use of white phosphorus by the IDF during its 2009 military campaign in Gaza, including strikes on schools, hospitals, and aid warehouses. Since Israel launched its counteroffensive, the Palestinian Health Ministry reports that 1,417 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, with 6,200 injured. Nearly one-third of the dead are children. In addition to airstrikes, Israel has imposed a complete blockade on food, water, fuel, and electricity to Gaza â measures some human rights groups argue violate international law. Human Rights Watch reports that white phosphorus was used in recent operations in Gaza and along the IsraelLebanon border, a practice that is unlawful in densely populated areas under international humanitarian law. All parties must protect civilians, allow humanitarian access, and uphold the laws of war.
